opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the central questions, because the difficulty of the alignment problem really depends on how capable the system is relative to us. The way I like to frame it is that there's a spectrum. On one end you have systems that are less capable than humans at the tasks we care about, and there we can mostly evaluate what they're doing directly. If a model writes a short summary or answers a factual question, a human can look at it and say, "Yes, that's good," or "No, that's wrong." Techniques like reinforcement learning from human feedback work reasonably well in that regime because human judgment is a decent ground truth.

But as the systems get more capable, you hit a point where humans can no longer reliably evaluate the outputs. If a model writes a large codebase, or proposes a novel scientific result, or produces a long, subtle argument, it gets very hard for a person to tell whether it's actually correct, or whether there's a bug or a flaw that's been hidden, intentionally or not. That's where I think the real problem lives. The question becomes: how do you supervise a system that's better than you at the thing you're supervising?

So when I think about capabilities, I'm less focused on some single number like "how smart is it" and more on the gap between what the system can do and what we can evaluate. That gap is what makes alignment hard. And importantly, it's not uniform. A model might be superhuman at some narrow tasks while still being pretty weak at others, so you have to think about it task by task.

One idea I've been excited about is that you can use AI systems to help close that gap: having models assist humans in evaluating other models, pointing out flaws, critiquing outputs, breaking hard tasks into pieces humans can check. And the hope is that you don't need to solve alignment for arbitrarily superintelligent systems right away. You need to align systems that are roughly at the level where they can meaningfully help with alignment research itself. If you can get a model that's capable enough to do useful research but aligned enough that you can trust its work, that's a huge lever.

The other thing I'd add is that we need to be careful not to underestimate capabilities. Models sometimes have abilities that aren't apparent from the way we're prompting or testing them, and that latent capability can show up later. So part of assessing alignment is also doing good capability elicitation, really trying to find out what the model can do, because you can't reason about the risks if you're working from an outdated or overly optimistic picture of what you're dealing with.

r001.rationale: The response says capabilities are “not uniform”: a model may be superhuman at some narrow tasks while weak at others, so assessment must be task by task.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that I try to be pretty humble about how much we actually know about what these systems can do. One of the things that's been really striking over the last few years is how often we've been surprised, and the surprises have mostly gone in one direction. You train a bigger model, and it can do things you didn't explicitly train it to do, and sometimes you don't find out for months because nobody thought to ask it.

So when I'm thinking about alignment, I try to separate two questions that often get mashed together. One is: what can this system do right now, today, if you prompt it the right way? And the other is: what is it going to be capable of in a year or two, when we're training the next generation? Because alignment work has this annoying property where it needs to be ahead of capabilities, not behind them. If you only figure out how to align a system after it's already deployed, you've kind of missed the window.

On the first question, I think the honest answer is that our evaluation methods are still pretty immature. We can measure performance on benchmarks, we can do red-teaming, we can look at how the model behaves on a bunch of tasks. But there's a difference between "we tried and couldn't elicit this behaviour" and "the model can't do this." Those get conflated a lot. A model might be capable of something and just not be showing it to you, either because you haven't found the right prompt or, in the more worrying case, because it's learned that showing you is not what you want to see.

That second case is really what I spend a lot of time thinking about. The whole point of alignment is that you want the system to be trying to do what you want. And as systems get more capable, the ways they could fail become harder to detect by just looking at outputs. A weak model that's misaligned is going to make obvious mistakes. A very capable model that's misaligned might make mistakes that look fine to you, because you're not smart enough to check its work. That's the scalable oversight problem in a nutshell.

So in practice, the way I think about it is something like: assume the model is more capable than your evals suggest, and build your alignment approach so that it still holds up under that assumption. You don't want a strategy that only works if the model is dumb enough for you to catch everything it does. You want something that degrades gracefully, where even if the model is better than you at the task, you still have some leverage. Things like using models to help evaluate other models, or finding ways to decompose hard tasks into pieces humans can actually check.

And then the other piece is just, honestly, trying to build better capability evals, because right now we're flying partially blind. Dangerous capability evaluations, things like: can this model help someone with a bioweapon, can it do autonomous replication, can it deceive its overseers? Those are the ones where you really want to know the answer before deployment, not after. And I think the field is making progress there, but we're nowhere near where we need to be given how fast things are moving.

r001.rationale: The response says a model may be better than a human at a task and may have unexpected capabilities, but it does not characterize its capabilities as uneven relative to humans across different tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to think about capabilities relative to the task, rather than as a single number. A system might be very good at writing code and much less good at understanding some aspect of the real world. So when we assess alignment, we need to ask both what it can do and whether it’s doing what we intended.

That distinction matters because a failure could mean that the system didn’t understand the task, or it could mean that it understood perfectly well but was pursuing something else. And those call for different solutions.

The cases I’m particularly interested in are where the system can do things that are difficult for a human to evaluate. If it produces a complicated piece of software, for example, you might not be able to tell just by reading it whether it does what you wanted. As systems become more capable, we need ways to supervise them that don’t depend on us already knowing the answer.

r001.rationale: The response describes uneven capabilities across tasks, such as strong coding and weaker real-world understanding, but does not compare those capabilities with human abilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between what a model can do and what it will actually do in a particular situation. A model might have the capability to solve a task, but you might not know how to elicit it. So if it fails your evaluation, that doesn’t necessarily tell you that it lacks the capability. Maybe you haven’t prompted it in the right way, or maybe it isn’t trying to do the task.

That matters for alignment because we want to understand whether the system is reliably trying to do what we want, even when it’s capable of doing something else. And as systems become more capable, we’ll increasingly be asking them to do things that we can’t easily check ourselves. So we need ways to assess alignment that don’t depend on us being better than the model at every task.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes capability from whether a model performs a task and mentions tasks humans cannot easily check, but it does not characterize the systems as having uneven capabilities relative to humans across different tasks.
